f.t: Akwesasne spans lands in Quebec, Ontario and New York State, and three separate but linked political bodies govern it.
Kanien'kéha, the Mohawk language, remains central to identity in Akwesasne and is actively taught in its schools.
Akwesasne means 'Land Where the Partridge Drums'.

n.l: Along the St. Lawrence River where Ontario, Quebec and New York State meet, in Canada and the United States

f.t: The Anishinabek Nation speaks for 39 First Nations in Ontario with about 70,000 citizens, roughly one third of the province's First Nation population.
It is Ontario's oldest political organization, with roots in the Confederacy of Three Fires that long predates European contact.
In 1949 the Nation set up the Union of Ontario Indians as its secretariat, replacing the Grand General Indian Council, which first met under that name in 1870.

n.l: 39 First Nations across Ontario, Canada, from Pikwàkanagàn in the east and Aamjiwnaang in the south to Lake Nipigon in the north

f.t: Young people aged 0 to 35 make up about 65 percent of the Atikamekw population today.
The Atikamekw language, like other Algonquin and Anishinaabe languages, is rich in imagery and names things by how they truly are.
The Atikamekw population has grown strongly since 1960.

n.l: Nitaskinan in central Quebec, Canada, with the communities of Manawan, Wemotaci and Opitciwan

f.t: The Dene Nation brings together five regional groups, the Gwich'in, Sahtú, Deh Cho, Tłı̨chǫ and Akaitcho Dene, each with its own language and territory.
In July 1975 more than 300 delegates meeting in Fort Simpson unanimously adopted the Dene Declaration, affirming the Dene as a distinct nation.
Dene simply means 'the people'. Their homeland, Denendeh, lies in the western Northwest Territories.

n.l: Denendeh, the western Northwest Territories, Canada

f.p: Grand Council of the Crees (Eeyou Istchee) / Cree Nation Government
f.t: The Cree of northern Quebec call themselves Eeyou. Their land, Eeyou Istchee, means the People's Land and includes eleven Cree communities.

f.p: Grand Council of the Crees (Eeyou Istchee) / Cree Nation Government
f.t: Eeyou Istchee is home to more than 20,000 people.

f.p: Grand Council of the Crees (Eeyou Istchee) / Cree Nation Government
f.t: Each Eeyou First Nation runs its own local government, and every elected Chief also sits on the board of the Grand Council of the Crees to address shared issues.

n.l: Eeyou Istchee, the lands east of James Bay and Hudson Bay in northern Quebec, Canada

f.t: About 18,000 people of Gitxsan heritage live around the world.
Gitxsanimaax, the traditional Gitxsan language, has two dialects: Giigeenix, spoken up river, and Gyeets, spoken down river.
Gitxsan society is matriarchal, with four clans made up of independent Houses (Huwilp), each led by a Wii Simoogit, or high chief.

n.l: The Laxyip along the upper Skeena River and its tributaries in northern British Columbia, Canada

f.t: The Council of the Haida Nation works to steward the lands and waters of Haida territories and carry Haida culture and language to future generations.
In April 2024 British Columbia and the Council of the Haida Nation signed the Rising Tide agreement, a first of its kind recognizing Haida Aboriginal title in Haida Gwaii.
Haida Gwaii is a group of more than 200 islands, about one million hectares, lying roughly 100 kilometres off northern British Columbia.

n.l: Haida Gwaii, an archipelago off the north coast of British Columbia, Canada

f.t: In 2025 Heiltsuk members ratified a written constitution, a milestone in self-governance.
Haíɫzaqv means 'to speak and act correctly', principles that guide Heiltsuk ancestral and present-day ways of life.
In 1997 the Supreme Court of Canada, in R. v. Gladstone, recognized a Heiltsuk Aboriginal right to harvest and sell herring spawn on kelp.

n.l: The Central Coast of British Columbia, Canada, centred on Bella Bella (Wáglísla) on Campbell Island

f.p: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, Indigenous Affairs and Reconciliation
f.t: The Innu Nation land claim, accepted for negotiation in 1978, covers about 70 percent of Labrador.
The Innu Nation represents about 3,200 Innu of Labrador, most of whom live in the communities of Sheshatshiu and Natuashish.

f.p: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, Indigenous Affairs and Reconciliation
f.t: In 2008 the Innu Nation and Newfoundland and Labrador signed the Tshash Petapen, or New Dawn, Agreement.

n.l: Nitassinan: Labrador (Newfoundland and Labrador) and eastern Quebec, Canada

f.t: Roughly 60 percent of Inuit can hold a conversation in Inuktut, the Inuit language.
Most Inuit in Canada live in 51 communities across Inuit Nunangat, a homeland covering about 40 percent of Canada's land and 72 percent of its coastline.
Inuit Nunangat, the Canadian Inuit name for the homeland, takes in land, water and ice, which Inuit see as integral to their culture and way of life.

n.l: Inuit Nunangat: the Inuvialuit Settlement Region, Nunavut, Nunavik and Nunatsiavut in Arctic Canada

f.t: Six communities lie within the Inuvialuit Settlement Region: Aklavik, Inuvik, Paulatuk, Sachs Harbour, Tuktoyaktuk and Ulukhaktok.
Signed on June 5, 1984, the Inuvialuit Final Agreement was the first comprehensive land claim agreement north of 60 degrees latitude, and only the second in Canada at the time.
One of the agreement's basic goals is keeping Inuvialuit cultural identity and values strong as northern society changes.

n.l: The Inuvialuit Settlement Region in the western Arctic, Northwest Territories and Yukon, Canada

f.t: About 8,000 people live in Kahnawà:ke, on the banks of the St. Lawrence River about 10 kilometres south of Montreal.
For more than a hundred years, many people from Kahnawà:ke, mostly men, have worked in the ironworking trade, much of it in the United States.
The name Kahnawà:ke literally means 'on the rapids', describing the eastern reaches of the territory.

n.l: On the south shore of the St. Lawrence River, near Montreal, Quebec, Canada

f.p: Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada
f.t: Kainai, the Blood Tribe, had 13,057 registered members as of September 2026.
In 2026 the Blood Tribe Land Management Department won a Prairie Conservation Award.
The Blood Tribe's stated mission is to preserve and protect its lands, culture, language and traditions in the spirit of Kainayssini.

n.l: Southern Alberta, Canada, with its main community at Standoff; part of the Blackfoot Confederacy

f.t: The Ktunaxa Nation Council helps represent the shared interests of four Ktunaxa First Nations within ʔamakʔis Ktunaxa, the Ktunaxa homelands.
Ktunaxa people have lived beside the Kootenay and Columbia Rivers and the Arrow Lakes for more than 10,000 years.
ʔamakʔis Ktunaxa, the traditional territory, covers about 70,000 square kilometres in the Kootenay region of southeastern British Columbia.

n.l: ʔamakʔis Ktunaxa: the Kootenay region of southeastern British Columbia, Canada, with Kootenay Tribes also based today in Montana and Idaho, United States

f.t: Many historic Métis communities still stand along rivers and lakes once tied to fur trade posts, and many Métis citizens live in cities within the Homeland.
The Métis emerged as a distinct Indigenous people with their own culture, traditions, nationhood and language, Michif.
The Métis National Council describes the Métis Nation Homeland as Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, plus parts of Ontario, BC, the Northwest Territories and the northern United States.

n.l: The Métis Nation Homeland as described by the Métis National Council: Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, plus parts of Ontario, British Columbia, the Northwest Territories and the northern United States

f.t: Mi'kmaw communities in Nova Scotia wrote their own Netukulimk Livelihood Management Plans so members who fish can support themselves and their families.
In 1999 the Marshall decision of the Supreme Court of Canada recognized the Treaties of 1760 and 1761, along with a right to hunt, fish and gather to earn a moderate livelihood.
In 2006 the 13 Mi'kmaw Chiefs of Nova Scotia formed the Assembly of Nova Scotia Mi'kmaw Chiefs to guide the Nation's negotiators on rights and title.

n.l: Mi’kma’ki: Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and the Gaspé in Canada, with relatives in Maine, United States

f.t: Muskeg Lake Cree Nation planned a gathering for August 20 to 23, 2026 to mark 150 years since Treaty 6 was signed.
The community credits its veterans, who served in both World Wars, Korea and peacetime, with shaping how Muskeg Lake developed.
In 1988 Muskeg Lake Cree Nation created Asimakeniseekan Askiy in Saskatoon, the first commercial urban reserve in Canada.

n.l: Treaty 6 territory in central Saskatchewan, Canada, with urban reserve land in Saskatoon

f.t: Musqueam is a strong, growing community of more than 1,300 members, many living on the Musqueam reserve near the mouth of the Fraser River.
For thousands of years, Musqueam ancestors have lived in the Fraser River estuary, an area that takes in much of today's Metro Vancouver.
The name xʷməθkʷəy̓əm means place of the məθkʷəy̓, a plant, and Musqueam people are traditionally hən̓q̓əmin̓əm̓ speakers.

n.l: The Fraser River estuary, including much of Metro Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada

f.t: The Nisg̱a’a, People of the Nass River, are a self-governing First Nation on Canada's Pacific Coast.
More than 360 fluent Nisg̱a’a speakers live in the Nation's villages, and the language is taught in Nisg̱a’a schools.
The Nisg̱a’a Final Agreement was the first modern treaty in British Columbia, and it recognizes both Nisg̱a’a Lands and the Nisg̱a’a Government.

n.l: The Nass River Valley (K’alii-Aksim-Lisims) in northwestern British Columbia, Canada

f.t: The Nunatsiavut Government offers an Inuttitut phrasebook app to encourage everyday speaking of the language in its communities.
Nunatsiavut's legislative capital is Hopedale and its administrative capital is Nain.
The Nunatsiavut Government, the self-government of Labrador Inuit, officially came into being on December 1, 2005.

n.l: Nunatsiavut, on the north coast of Labrador, Canada

f.t: Language retention among Nunavik Inuit is over 95 percent, and Inuktitut remains the main language spoken in the region.
More than 10,000 Inuit live in Nunavik, in 15 villages along Ungava Bay, Hudson Strait and Hudson Bay.
Makivvik, an Inuktitut name meaning 'to rise up', protects Nunavik Inuit rights under the 1975 James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement, Canada's first comprehensive Inuit land claim.

n.l: Nunavik, northern Quebec, Canada: 15 villages along Hudson Bay, Hudson Strait and Ungava Bay

f.t: Under the agreement Inuit own about 350,000 square kilometres of land, including about 35,000 square kilometres with mineral rights.
Nunavut became Canada's newest territory on April 1, 1999, and Inuktitut is an official language of its government with Inuinnaqtun, English and French.
Signed on May 25, 1993, the Nunavut Agreement is the biggest Aboriginal land claims agreement ever made in Canada.

n.l: Nunavut, Canada: the Qikiqtaaluk, Kivalliq and Kitikmeot regions

f.t: The Nuu-chah-nulth Tribal Council serves fourteen Nuu-chah-nulth First Nations with about 10,000 members, grouped in three regions.
The Council's vision is self-government that builds strong, healthy Nuu-chah-nulth communities.
The Council publishes Ha-Shilth-Sa, Canada's oldest First Nations newspaper and the newspaper of record of the Nuu-chah-nulth people.

n.l: The west coast of Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada

f.p: Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada
f.t: Piikani Nation had 3,928 registered members as of September 2026.
Piikani stories, ceremonies and songs describe an ancestral territory reaching north to the North Saskatchewan River and west into the Rocky Mountains.
The international border divides the Piikani into the Aapatohsipiikani, or North Piikani, in Canada and the Amsskapipiikani, or South Piikani, in the United States.

n.l: Around Brocket in southern Alberta, Canada, near the Old Man River; part of the Blackfoot Confederacy

f.t: The Shuswap Nation Tribal Council brings together nine Secwépemc communities in the Southern Interior of British Columbia.
Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc works to make Secwépemctsín the primary language of communication, education, government and business in its territory.
Secwépemc Chiefs formed the Shuswap Nation Tribal Council in 1980 to advance Aboriginal rights, self-government and the settlement of land title.

n.l: Secwepemcúl’ecw, a large territory in the interior of British Columbia, Canada, stretching from the Columbia River valley west to the Fraser River

f.t: Siksika Nation has about 7,800 members, and its language is Siksika, or Blackfoot.
Siksika's coat of arms, registered with the Canadian Heraldic Authority in June 1992, was the first registered by any Nation in Canada.
Treaty 7 was signed in 1877 at Blackfoot Crossing, on Siksika land.

n.l: East of Calgary, Alberta, Canada; part of the Blackfoot Confederacy

f.p: Six Nations of the Grand River
f.t: It is the only First Nation community home to all six Haudenosaunee nations: Mohawk, Cayuga, Onondaga, Oneida, Seneca and Tuscarora.

f.p: Six Nations of the Grand River
f.t: No First Nation in Canada has a larger population than Six Nations of the Grand River.

f.p: Six Nations of the Grand River
f.t: Each nation's own name carries meaning: the Mohawk are the People of the Flint, the Onondaga the People of the Hills, the Cayuga the People of the Great Swamp.

n.l: Along the Grand River in southern Ontario, Canada
n.n: Six Nations of the Grand River

f.t: Sḵwx̱wú7mesh traditional territory covers 6,732 square kilometres and includes 23 villages.
The Squamish language is a sign of resilience: dozens of Nation members are learning it from their Elders as a second language.
The Nation's roots lie in several communities that became one government in 1923. Most members live on Vancouver's North Shore, others along the Squamish River.

n.l: The North Shore of Vancouver and the Squamish River valley, British Columbia, Canada

f.t: Historically the Okanagan Nation Alliance represented eight member communities: seven in Canada and the Colville Confederated Tribes in Washington State.
The Okanagan Nation Alliance reports that the new Okanagan Dam Fish Passage, after years of advocacy and planning, lets salmon reach Okanagan Lake for the first time in nearly 100 years.
In 1846 the border that now divides Canada and the United States was drawn across Syilx territory without the Nation's consent, separating lands and families.

n.l: The Okanagan, Similkameen and Nicola areas of British Columbia, Canada, and northern Washington State, United States

f.p: Government of the Northwest Territories, Executive and Indigenous Affairs
f.t: The Tłı̨chǫ Government makes laws for its citizens in areas including education, child and family services, and Tłı̨chǫ language and culture.

f.p: Government of the Northwest Territories, Executive and Indigenous Affairs
f.t: The agreement gave the Tłı̨chǫ ownership of a single 39,000 square kilometre block of land, including subsurface resources, around their four communities.

f.p: Government of the Northwest Territories, Executive and Indigenous Affairs
f.t: The Tłı̨chǫ Agreement, in effect since August 4, 2005, was the first combined land, resources and self-government agreement in the Northwest Territories.

n.l: Between Great Slave Lake and Great Bear Lake in the Northwest Territories, Canada, around the communities of Behchokǫ̀, Whatì, Gamètì and Wekweètì

f.t: Tsleil-Waututh people see caring for the lands and waters of their territory as a birthright and obligation, so future generations can thrive.
Tsleil-Waututh means 'People of the Inlet'. The Nation's language is hən̓q̓əmin̓əm, in which its name is səlilwətaɬ.
The community is centred on Burrard Inlet in North Vancouver, while ancestral lands covered about 1,865 square kilometres.

n.l: Burrard Inlet (səlilwət) in North Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada

f.t: Tsuut'ina Nation describes itself today as a highly sufficient and economically advanced First Nation.
Elders interpret the name Tsuut'ina as 'many people' or 'beaver people', and both meanings are considered correct.
Tsuut'ina is the only Dene-speaking nation in Treaty 7 territory, linked to the wider Dene Nation by its Athabaskan language.

n.l: Treaty 7 territory in southern Alberta, Canada, bordering the city of Calgary

f.t: Old Crow, a fly-in community of about 300 people on the Porcupine River, is the seat of the Vuntut Gwitchin government.
The Van Tat Gwich'in homeland covers about 55,548 square kilometres of northern Yukon, along the migration routes of the Porcupine caribou herd.
Dinjii Zhuh k'yuu, the Gwich'in language, is the official language of the Vuntut Gwitchin First Nation, which is training teachers and raising young speakers.

n.l: Old Crow and the surrounding homeland in northern Yukon, Canada

f.t: The Nation counts more than 300 Wendat businesses, including many artisans, artists and cultural organizations.
The Wendat Nation has 5,233 members. About 1,495 live in Wendake and the rest live elsewhere in Quebec, in other provinces and in other countries.
After the Wendat language went dormant in the 1800s, the Yawenda project (2007 to 2012) brought language specialists and community members together to revive it.

n.l: Wendake, near Québec City, within the traditional territory Onyionhwentsïio’ in Quebec, Canada

f.t: Six Wolastoqey communities in New Brunswick, Matawaskiye, Neqotkuk, Pilick, Sitansisk, Welamukotuk and Wotstak, work together through the Wolastoqey Nation in New Brunswick.
The Supreme Court of Canada has ruled that the Peace and Friendship Treaties remain legally binding, and they are the foundation of Wolastoqey treaty rights.
The Wolastoqiyik are the people of the Wolastoq watershed, a homeland of land, sea and fresh water reaching from the Bay of Fundy to the St. Lawrence River.

n.l: The Wolastoq (Saint John River) watershed, from the Bay of Fundy to the St. Lawrence: New Brunswick and Quebec in Canada, and Maine in the United States
